name: Marco Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead picker at Northgate Grocers, a big supermarket with a busy online-order side. Most days I run the pick team of eight, walking the aisles with a scanner and a trolley rack, filling click-and-collect and home-delivery orders. On Saturdays I'm on the tills because the shop is rammed. I start at seven, check the order queue and sort out substitutions when something's out of stock.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and do you use any AI tools yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the pace, to be honest. It's like a game with a clock, and I'm among the fastest in the building, about a hundred and ten items an hour. What wears me out is the heavy stuff, water crates and cat litter, and customers who complain that the substitute isn't the same brand of oat milk. I use AI tools every day. I have one that helps me write quick replies to customers, another that turns the day's order list into the best walking route, and I use a chatbot to learn things like spreadsheets. My girlfriend Priya is a nurse on a hospital ward, and we've got about fourteen months of costs saved, because we both hate debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the tools I'm using are enough and I'd rather things settle down. At work I'd carry on teaching the new pickers the route tool. Online I'd probably post a joke about all the doom predictions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'm fine and I carry on. My job is physical and fast, and the routing tool just makes me faster. The one thing in my head is that the online side is where the supermarket wants to grow, so I'm well placed if it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and apply for the operations supervisor role that's coming up in the spring. I'd carry on with the AI tools, and I'd put away about six hundred a month with Priya for a house deposit. I'd also finish the spreadsheet course I started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a steady one. I like when the plan is simply to keep doing well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the supervisor role mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eight thousand more a year, a desk for part of the day and fewer heavy lifts. It's the sort of job where you plan the day's pick instead of just doing it. I'd be good at it because I know where the problems come from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you teach a new picker to use the route tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd walk them round once and show how the order of items changes the time. Then I'd let them try it on their own. People learn better when a tool saves their own legs, so I walk a new picker round once and then let them try.

say: I'd say the tools I use are **enough** and I'd rather things settle.
I'd carry on teaching new pickers the **route** tool.
think: My job is physical and fast, and the routing tool only makes me **faster**.
The online side is where the supermarket wants to **grow**, which suits me.
do: Apply for the operations **supervisor** role this spring.
Put about six hundred a month away for a house **deposit**.
feel: **Calm**, because the plan is just to keep doing well.
S0.quote: People learn better when a tool saves their own legs, so I walk a new picker round once and then let them try.
fieldNote: Calm fits a strong **cushion**, a fast and valued job, and a habit of using the tools every day.
The **supervisor** role is a ladder he can already see.

steps.text: Apply for the operations supervisor role this spring
Put six hundred a month towards a house deposit
Finish the spreadsheet course
Keep leading the pick team of eight

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should get on with it and use the tools well. At work I'd run a short session for the team on what the software does. Online I'd share tips, and maybe argue a bit with someone who says it's all a scam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is closer to home. Thinking tasks first means the customer chat, the substitutions, the ordering and the planning, and that's where Northgate would use it. Picking itself would stay human for now, but there would be fewer pickers per hundred orders because the route tool and software do more. I'd rather be the person who sets up the software at Northgate than the person it replaces. I think I'm safe if I'm the one who runs the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to be the person who sets up and checks the new substitution software, so I'm part of the change. I'd go for the supervisor job and then for an ops analyst job, the people who look at the data. I'd keep up the courses, put more into savings, and probably start a small side thing, reselling limited trainers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, actually a bit excited. A bit uneasy for my team, because not everyone would move with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your team would struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dennis, who's fifty and has been picking for twenty years. He's fast but doesn't trust screens. And two part-timers who only do ten hours a week. I'd help them, but I can't carry people forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the trainer reselling thing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I buy limited releases when they drop and resell them for a bit more. It's about two hundred a month profit now. It's small, but it's mine, and it's something I'd grow if my hours dropped.

say: I'd say we should get on with it and use the tools **well**.
I'd run a short **session** for the team on what the software does.
think: The thinking tasks, like chat and **substitutions**, would move to software first.
I'm safe if I'm the one who **runs** the tools.
do: Ask to set up and check the new **substitution** software.
Go for the supervisor role and then **ops analyst**.
Grow my trainer **reselling** side business, about two hundred a month now.
feel: **Excited**, with some unease for teammates who won't move.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the person who sets up the software at Northgate than the person it replaces.
fieldNote: He stays calm **because** he sits close to the tools and expects to be the one who runs them.
His worry is for **colleagues** like Dennis, who don't trust screens, and he says he can't carry people forever.

steps.text: Ask to set up and check Northgate's new substitution software
Apply for supervisor, then ops analyst
Grow trainer reselling beyond two hundred a month
Raise monthly savings to eight hundred

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready, and the shops and the government have two years to show up. At work I'd tell the team to learn what they can and to stick together. Online I'd probably share everything and try to organise a few people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is where I get anxious. Online picking is exactly what robots in a warehouse would do, and the robots arrive around 2031. I'm safe from the thinking AI for a while, but my entire speciality is the bit that disappears. I'd have to move, and fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move into the part that runs the machines: robot supervisor, systems, stock data. I'd ask Northgate to put me on any pilot with picking robots, and learn how they break. Priya and I would save as hard as we can, stop eating out and put off the house. And I'd push the reselling, because it's the one income that's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but ready to move. It'd feel like standing at the start of a race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask to join the robot pilot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If robots are coming to Northgate, I'd rather help install them than watch them take my job. I'd learn how they work, what goes wrong and what they can't do. Then when they need a human, I'm the one who knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Priya feel if you lost the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd worry, but her ward is short of nurses and her pay is steady. She'd say we'll be fine, and she'd mean it. We'd just put the house on hold and live on her wage plus savings.

say: I'd say we're not **ready** and the government has two years to show up.
I'd tell the team to learn what they can and **stick together**.
think: Online picking is exactly what **warehouse robots** do, around 2031.
My whole speciality is the part that **disappears**.
do: Ask Northgate to put me on any **robot** pilot and learn how they break.
Save hard with Priya and **postpone** the house.
Push the trainer **reselling** as a second income.
feel: **Anxious**, but ready to move, like the start of a race.
S2.quote: If robots are coming to Northgate, I'd rather help install them than watch them take my job.
fieldNote: **Picking** is the most automatable part of his job, yet he turns that fear into a plan within a minute.
Priya's steady **nursing** pay and fourteen months of savings keep him short of alarmed.

steps.text: Ask to join Northgate's picking-robot pilot
Learn robot maintenance and stock data on evenings
Postpone the house and save hard with Priya
Push trainer reselling as a second income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long enough warning to be useful and short enough to matter. At work I'd start an informal group on tools and training. Online I'd share what I find, keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel pretty okay for the first couple of years, and then the pressure builds toward 2034 when the robots can do picking. With five years I can learn, apply for the supervisor job and get into operations, so I'm not at the sharp end when it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the supervisor job, then ops analyst, and finish a part-time degree or certificate in supply chain. I'd keep up with the AI tools and teach them. I'd save eight hundred a month with Priya and aim for a smaller house, and have a kid around thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but good. It's the one where doing something now clearly pays off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why supply chain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's the thinking side of what I do now, planning how goods get from the lorry to the customer. Robots can pick, but someone still has to decide what to order and where it all goes. And the AI tools can help me learn it faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still have children with this hanging over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a bit later maybe, but yes. Priya and I would make sure one of us had a job that's hard to replace, and she has one. I'd say it's about being prepared, not about waiting.

say: I'd call it a long enough warning to be **useful**.
I'd start an informal **group** on tools and training.
think: The pressure builds toward **2034**, when robots can pick.
With five years I can learn and move to **operations** before it hits.
do: Move to **supervisor**, then ops analyst, and finish a supply chain certificate.
Save eight hundred a month with Priya for a smaller **house**.
feel: **Uneasy** but good, because acting now clearly pays off.
S3.quote: Robots can pick, but someone still has to decide what to order and where it all goes.
fieldNote: Five years suits an **adaptive** person: he turns unease into a clear ladder from picking to planning.
Priya's hard-to-**replace** nursing job gives him the confidence to plan a family.

steps.text: Move up to supervisor, then ops analyst
Finish a part-time supply chain certificate
Save eight hundred a month with Priya
Plan a child around thirty, with Priya's job secure

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is generous and I'd use it. At work I'd tell younger pickers not to think of picking as the end of the road. Online I'd probably post that people should learn something new every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me ten years is a lot of time to switch lanes. By 2036 I could be a supply chain manager or running my own business, and the robots come in 2039. I'm adaptable, so I'd feel good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep up the AI habits, take the supervisor job, and do a supply chain degree part time. I'd build the reselling into a proper small shop, with a website. I'd buy a modest house in about five years and have a kid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little buzzing. It's the sort of world where I can plan and still enjoy my days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the website business sell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Limited-edition trainers and streetwear, bought and sold on a small scale. I'd use AI for listings and product photos and write the descriptions myself. It could become a few hundred a month, then a thousand, if I'm careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in ten years that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who don't move. I'd keep thinking about Dennis and others like him. A decade is a gift if you use it and a trap if you don't, and I can't make anyone else use it.

say: I'd say ten years is **generous** and I'd use it.
I'd tell younger pickers that picking is not the end of the **road**.
think: Ten years is plenty of time to **switch** lanes.
By 2036 I could be a supply chain **manager** or running my own business.
do: Take the supervisor job and study **supply chain** part time.
Build the reselling into a small **website** shop.
Buy a modest house in about five years and have a **kid**.
feel: **Calm**, a little buzzing, able to plan and enjoy my days.
S4.quote: A decade is a gift if you use it and a trap if you don't, and I can't make anyone else use it.
fieldNote: His calm comes from **adaptability**, fourteen months of savings and a clear ladder, rather than from ignoring risk.
He still **worries** about colleagues who will not use the decade.

steps.text: Take the supervisor job and move into planning
Study supply chain part time
Build the reselling into a small website shop
Buy a modest house in about five years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because picking is the exact kind of work robots do best and I'd have no time to move. What would help is notice, so we can plan, and paid time to retrain without losing pay. And a company that tells the pickers early rather than the day before.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'm among the fastest pickers in the building, but the person who sets up the software is the one who gets to keep going. Maybe just that people who work in supermarkets aren't all afraid of technology. A lot of us use it daily, and we'd like to be asked how to use it well, not told when it's been decided.

headlineQuote: I'm among the fastest pickers in the building, but the person who sets up the software is the one who gets to keep going.
portrait: **Marco** is a 27-year-old lead picker and weekend cashier at Northgate Grocers, running an eight-person online-order team.
He is centre politically and adaptive, using **AI** every day for routes, replies and learning.
His girlfriend Priya is a **nurse**, and they have about fourteen months of costs saved.
He moves from calm to **anxious** when robots could take over picking by 2031, and answers each time with a practical plan.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** case, because picking is the work robots do best and there'd be no time to move.
whatWouldHelp: **Notice**, paid time to retrain, and being asked how to use the tools well.
